newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA SEEN EASING FRANKING CREDIT RULE - SOURCES.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA SEEN EASING FRANKING CREDIT RULE - SOURCES.

text.p: Treasurer Peter Costello is expected to announce as soon as this week that the government has backed away from its 1997/98 budget proposal to severely restrict the use of dividend franking credits by investors and fund managers, sources told Reuters.
Costello approved a new set of proposals in the past few days after receiving recommendations from his own department and the Australian Taxation Office about 10 days ago, the sources said.

The new proposals, which have been held up in Parliament House due to the illness of Prime Minister John Howard, effectively overturn the controversial May 13 budget announcement that immediately removed franking credits from investors who hedged within 45 days of buying the stock.

Meetings between industry representatives and the two government departments earlier this month led to an agreement that superannuation fund managers be allowed to hedge on the downside only, along with a "delta measurement test" where an average yield return was to be calculated.
If the fund managers passed this test they could use hedging techniques to protect their portfolio within the 45-day period.

"The 45 day rule is likely to have a couple of major concessions or exclusions in it, which mean that protection on the downside is okay and that certain options and futures transactions might be okay if the delta is less than point-seven," one industry source said.

"The Treasurer, I am reliably informed, has greenlighted those recommendations but the measures are floating around somewhere in the Treasury, the Treasurer's office or in the deputy Prime Minister's office."
With John Howard recovering from influenza, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer is running the country until the end of the week.
A government source said the two departments had agreed to water down the budget proposals and believed there could be an announcement from the Treasurer by the end of next week.
The budget plan did not contain any revenue estimates but warned that the revenue base needed to be protected from any expansion of tax minimisation practices.

Its main objective was to remove the appeal of "dividend washing" schemes where franking credits on stocks held by foreigners are made available to local investors who use them to reduce their overall tax bill.
